442.title: Get out, Mara
442.hook: Moggallana feels Mara in his belly and tells him to come out
442.howItsDone: In several early Buddhist stories, Mara leaves once he is recognized ('I know you, Mara'); some meditation teachers use this as a model for noting or naming difficult mind-states without suppressing them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the god who thought he was permanent, and your line, nothing is forever. Did the line make you a little more attentive to someone you love? Day four hundred forty-two.

A heaviness in the stomach can arrive for no clear reason. Dread before a meeting. A sourness after a phone call. It's easy to carry it around all afternoon without ever asking what it is. One day the monk Moggallana was walking up and down in the open air, practicing, and his belly suddenly felt heavy, as if it were full of beans. He stopped. He went inside, sat down, and looked. Today: get out, Mara.
screen: `A HEAVINESS IN THE STOMACH.` → `MOGGALLANA, WALKING IN THE OPEN.` → `HE STOPS, SITS, AND LOOKS.`

segments.voice: This is the fiftieth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the rebuke to Mara. Mara is the tempter of the Buddhist stories: the voice of distraction, fear and craving, sometimes told as a being, sometimes heard as a force in the mind. Yesterday he hid in a god's assembly. Here, the text says, he had slipped into Moggallana's belly. Moggallana sits, turns his attention inward, and sees him there. And he speaks plainly: come out, Evil One. Come out. Don't trouble the Buddha or the Buddha's disciple, or it will bring you harm and suffering for a long time. Mara thinks: he doesn't really know me. Even his teacher wouldn't recognize me that fast. And Moggallana answers his thought: I know you. Don't think I don't. So Mara comes out of Moggallana's mouth and stands leaning against the door bar. And Moggallana says: I see you there too. Then he tells Mara an old story. Long ago, he says, I was a Mara myself, named Dusi, and you were my sister's son, my nephew. He tells what happened when that Mara tormented a Buddha of an earlier age, and how it ended badly for him. Mara, the text says, is dismayed, and disappears. Look at how the scene works. Moggallana doesn't fight. He doesn't panic. He doesn't pretend the heaviness isn't there. He stops, sits, looks, and names it. I see you. And what is seen clearly often loosens its grip. Some meditation teachers call this naming: seeing a mood clearly and calling it what it is, without fighting it.
screen: `MARA: A TEMPTER, OR A FORCE IN THE MIND` · `COME OUT, EVIL ONE` · `I SEE YOU THERE TOO` · `STOP, SIT, LOOK, NAME` · then, large: `I SEE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one visiting mood. Sit, and scan the body slowly: the jaw, the shoulders, the chest, the belly. If you find a weight, a tightness, a flutter, stop there. Ask quietly, what are you? Worry? Irritation? Sadness? Let a name come. Say it inwardly, simply: I see you. Don't push it out. Let it stand by the door, seen. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Get out. The heart of Moggallana's plain words to Mara, come out, spoken only after he had stopped, looked, and seen him clearly. Today's word.
Your line: I see you. Today, when a mood moves in uninvited, stop for one breath, name it, and say the line. Day four hundred forty-two.

options: walk faster to shake it off.
go inside, sit down, and look at it.
ignore it and finish the walk.

what it means: Mara is often undone by being clearly seen and named: I know you.

443.title: People are a thicket
443.hook: an elephant trainer says animals are easy to read, people a tangle
443.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use MN 51's four kinds of persons to reflect on harm and harmlessness, and to point to the person who torments neither self nor others as the ideal of the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: get out, Mara, and your line, I see you. When a mood moved in, did you stop and name it? Day four hundred forty-three.

Dog people will tell you a dog can't lie. When it's happy, the whole back half wags. When it's guilty, it can't meet your eyes. People are harder. A smile can mean anything. A yes can mean no. A fine can mean please ask again. A son of an elephant trainer named Pessa once sat with the Buddha and said exactly this, from long experience with animals much bigger than dogs. Today: people are a thicket.
screen: `A DOG CAN'T LIE.` → `A SMILE CAN MEAN ANYTHING.` → `PESSA, THE ELEPHANT TRAINER'S SON.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Kandaraka, a wanderer who came along with Pessa. Pessa says something honest. People are a tangle, a thicket. Animals are an open clearing. I can train an elephant, he says, and in the time it takes to go to the town and back, it will show me every trick and dodge it has. But the people who work in my house do one thing with their bodies, say another thing with their words, and have something else again in their minds. The Buddha agrees: that's so, Pessa. People are a thicket. Then he offers a way to see through the tangle, not by reading faces, but by watching what people do to themselves and to others. There are four kinds of people. One torments himself: harsh practices that hurt only his own body. One torments others: the hunter, the butcher, the jailer, the one whose living is other people's pain. One torments both: a king, say, who holds a great sacrifice that exhausts himself and drives his servants with sticks and fear. And one torments neither: who lives, here and now, cool and at peace. Pessa is delighted and leaves early, with somewhere to be. The Buddha says: if he had stayed a little longer, he would have gained a great deal. We all know Pessa's problem. People are hard to read. But the Buddha's answer isn't to become a better mind reader. It's to look at the harm and the ease people bring, and to ask which of the four we are becoming ourselves.
screen: `PEOPLE ARE A TANGLE; ANIMALS ARE OPEN` · `BODY, WORDS AND MIND DON'T MATCH` · `FOUR KINDS: WHO DO THEY TORMENT?` · `THE ONE WHO TORMENTS NEITHER` · then, large: `PEOPLE ARE THICKETS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one person gently. Think of someone who confuses you: what they say doesn't match what they do. Sit, and don't try to solve them. Just ask the Buddha's question, softly: where is the pain in their life, toward themselves, toward others? Let some compassion for the tangle come up. Then turn the question once toward yourself, without blame. Then rest with the breath, open as a clearing. The bell holds the time.
People are a thicket. An elephant trainer's son's honest line: animals are open, people are tangled. The Buddha agrees, and offers four kinds of people to read by. Today's word.
Your line: people are thickets. Today, when someone's words and actions don't match, give them the patience you'd give a tangle, and watch what they do. Day four hundred forty-three.

what it means: look past faces to what people do: whom they harm, and whether they've found ease.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 51, Kandaraka Sutta (the discourse to Kandaraka)

444.title: Eleven doors
444.hook: like a burning house with eleven doors, there are many ways out
444.howItsDone: Buddhist meditation traditions offer many entry points, from breath-based concentration to loving-kindness and the other divine abodes, and some teachers match a practice to a student's temperament.

segments.voice: Yesterday: people are a thicket, and your line, people are thickets. Did you give someone the patience you'd give a tangle? Day four hundred forty-four.

A householder named Dasama, from a town called Atthakanagara, comes to the city of Pataliputta on business. Business done, he travels on to Vesali, looking for the monk Ananda. He has a single question, and he wants a single answer. Is there one thing, he asks, just one, which, if someone practices it diligently, frees the mind? He's hoping for the one key. Ananda gives him eleven. Today: eleven doors.
screen: `DASAMA, IN PATALIPUTTA ON BUSINESS.` → `IS THERE ONE THING THAT FREES THE MIND?` → `ANANDA GIVES HIM ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-second discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the man from Atthakanagara. Ananda answers: yes, there is one thing. Then he names it in eleven forms. Someone enters the first meditative absorption, and sees it clearly: this too is put together, made by intention, and whatever is made is impermanent and will end. Standing on that insight, the mind is freed. The same, Ananda says, with the second absorption, the third, the fourth. The same with loving-kindness, compassion, gladness for others and equanimity, the four divine abodes. The same with three formless states: boundless space, boundless consciousness, and nothingness. Eleven in all. The door isn't the state itself. It's seeing that even this lovely state is made, and so will pass. Dasama is overjoyed. He says: it's as if a man looking for one entrance to a hidden treasure found eleven at once. Or like a man whose house has eleven doors: if the house caught fire, he could escape through any one of them. Then he does something very practical. He gathers the monks of Vesali and Pataliputta, feeds them with his own hands, gives each a pair of robes, gives Ananda a set of three robes, and has a dwelling built for him. There's a quiet comfort in this. Dasama wanted one way out, the right one. He found eleven. Some readers hear in it a path with doors for many kinds of minds: stillness, kindness, spaciousness. Any door, opened with clear seeing, leads out.
screen: `ONE THING? YES, IN ELEVEN FORMS` · `FOUR ABSORPTIONS, FOUR DIVINE ABODES` · `SEE THAT EVEN THIS IS MADE` · `A BURNING HOUSE WITH ELEVEN DOORS` · then, large: `ELEVEN DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one door out. Choose one of Ananda's doors for this sit: stillness with the breath, kindness toward someone, or the sense of open space around you. Settle into it for a minute. Let it become pleasant. Then, gently, see what Dasama learned: this calm was made, by sitting, by breathing, by intention, and it will change. Rest in that seeing, without pushing the calm away. The bell holds the time.
Eleven doors. Four absorptions, four divine abodes, three formless states, each a way out of a burning house when seen as made and passing. Today's word.
Your line: eleven doors. Today, if one way to calm isn't working, try another door, a kind thought, a walk, a breath, without calling yourself a failure. Day four hundred forty-four.

screen: `DAY 444 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HEN ON HER EGGS.`

what it means: there are many doors; what opens each one is seeing that the state is made and will pass.

445.title: The hen on her eggs
445.hook: Ananda: keep practice warm like a hen on her eggs, and the chicks break out
445.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the hen simile to encourage steady, patient daily practice without straining for results; in MN 53 a senior disciple teaches while the Buddha rests and listens.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eleven doors, and your line, eleven doors. When one way to calm didn't work, did you try another door? Day four hundred forty-five.

The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, the Buddha's own people, have built a brand-new assembly hall. Nobody has used it yet. They ask the Buddha to be the first, to bless it with a teaching. He comes, and teaches late into the night. Then his back begins to ache. So he turns to Ananda and asks him to go on teaching, while he lies down on his right side, mindful, and rests. Ananda, with the Buddha listening, takes the floor. Today: the hen on her eggs.
screen: `A NEW HALL IN KAPILAVATTHU.` → `THE BUDDHA'S BACK ACHES.` → `ANANDA TAKES THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-third discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse on the disciple in training. Ananda speaks to Mahanama, a Sakyan noble, about someone who isn't finished yet but is on the way. They keep the precepts. They guard the senses. They eat in moderation. They stay wakeful for practice. They have faith, conscience, care, learning, energy, mindfulness and wisdom. And they can reach the four deep absorptions when they wish. Then Ananda gives a picture from any farmyard. A hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. She sits on them properly, keeps them warm, broods them well. She doesn't have to wish: oh, may my chicks break out of their shells with their claws and beaks. If she keeps sitting, they will break out, safely, on their own. So it is, Ananda says, with someone who keeps these qualities warm. They're able to break through. The hen doesn't push the chicks. She doesn't crack the shells for them. She doesn't lie awake worrying about hatching. Her whole job is to stay on the eggs. Breaking out is the eggs' business. The same picture appears in another discourse too, where the Buddha himself uses it. And when Ananda finishes, the Buddha sits up and says: good, Ananda, good. You've taught the disciple in training well. On an ordinary Tuesday, the picture still holds. You can't force the breakthrough. You can only keep the practice warm, day after day, and trust what warmth does.
screen: `THE DISCIPLE IN TRAINING` · `PRECEPTS, SENSES, FOOD, WAKEFULNESS` · `A HEN SITS ON HER EGGS` · `THE CHICKS BREAK OUT ON THEIR OWN` · then, large: `THE HEN ON THE EGGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one practice warm. Pick something you've been doing on this path: this daily sit, a kindness, a precept, an honest word. Sit, and simply stay with the breath, the way a hen stays on her eggs. Don't check for results. Don't wish for hatching. Each time the mind wanders off to ask is this working, come back and settle down on the eggs again. The bell holds the time.
The hen on her eggs. Ananda's picture of practice: keep it warm and steady, and what's ready to break out will break out. Today's word.
screen: `THE HEN ON HER EGGS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the hen on the eggs. Today, do your practice even if nothing seems to happen, and leave the hatching to the eggs. Day four hundred forty-five.

fork.reveal: Ananda's hen keeps sitting. without wishing or forcing, the chicks break out safely when they're ready.

what it means: keep the practice warm and steady; breaking through is what warmth does, in its time.

what a scholar hears: the hen simile appears in more than one discourse, including MN 16, where the Buddha uses it of a monk who has cleared away the mind's barriers and shackles and so is able to break through.

Majjhima Nikaya 16, Cetokhila Sutta (the hen simile)

446.title: The bare bone
446.hook: sense pleasures satisfy like a bare bone to a hungry dog
446.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use MN 54's similes, such as the bare bone and the grass torch, in reflections on the drawbacks of sense pleasures, pointing practitioners toward a deeper contentment in meditation and ethical living.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hen on her eggs, and your line, the hen on the eggs. Did you keep one practice warm, even when nothing seemed to happen? Day four hundred forty-six.

Best clothes, a parasol, sandals: Potaliya, a householder, walks up to the Buddha dressed for an occasion. When the Buddha calls him householder, he bristles. I'm not a householder anymore, he says. I've given my wealth to my children. I've cut myself off from all worldly affairs. I just live on food and clothing. The Buddha says, gently: that isn't what cutting off means in this teaching. Potaliya wants to know what is. Today: the bare bone.
screen: `POTALIYA, PARASOL AND SANDALS.` → `I'VE CUT OFF ALL AFFAIRS.` → `THAT ISN'T WHAT CUTTING OFF MEANS.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-fourth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Potaliya. The Buddha says real cutting off is inward: giving up killing, stealing, lying, slander, greed, spite, anger and arrogance. Then he turns to sense pleasures, and gives a run of pictures. The first is the one people remember. A dog, weak with hunger, waits by a butcher's shop. The butcher throws it a bone, scraped clean of meat, with only a smear of blood on it. The dog gnaws and gnaws. Does that bone take away its hunger? No, says Potaliya. It only gets the dog tired and frustrated. Sense pleasures are like that bone, says the Buddha: much pain, much disappointment, more danger in them than delight. They taste of something, and they leave the hunger where it was. He gives more pictures. A bird flying off with a scrap of meat, chased by other birds who peck and claw at it until it lets go. A grass torch carried into the wind, burning the hand that holds it. A dream of a lovely park that's gone when you wake. Goods borrowed for show, which the owners come and take back. Notice what he isn't saying. He isn't saying the bone is evil, or that a dog is foolish to want food. Hunger is real. The point is that some things only look like food. You can gnaw them all day and stay hungry. And Potaliya, who came in claiming he had cut everything off, finds he had only cut off his wealth.
screen: `REAL CUTTING OFF IS INWARD` · `A HUNGRY DOG AND A BARE BONE` · `A BIRD, A TORCH, A DREAM, A LOAN` · `SOME THINGS ONLY LOOK LIKE FOOD` · then, large: `A BARE BONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: spot one bone you gnaw. Sit, and think of something you return to again and again, hoping it'll fill you: scrolling, snacking, checking, shopping, replaying an argument. Picture the last time. Did it take the hunger away, or leave you tired? Don't scold yourself. A hungry dog isn't bad. Just see the bone clearly. Then ask what real food would be for that hunger, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The bare bone. A bone scraped clean, thrown to a hungry dog: something that tastes like food and leaves you hungry. Today's word.
Your line: a bare bone. Today, when you catch yourself gnawing at something that never fills you, say the line, and set the bone down for a minute. Day four hundred forty-six.

what it means: some pleasures are like a bare bone: they taste of something and never fill the hunger they promise to.

447.title: Jivaka and meat
447.hook: the physician asks about meat; the monks' rule: not if seen, heard or suspected killed for them
447.howItsDone: Theravada monastics follow the threefold rule from MN 55 and the Vinaya, accepting what is offered; Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monastics keep a vegetarian diet, as do some lay Buddhists; in Tibetan communities practice varies, and some teachers encourage vegetarianism.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bare bone, and your line, a bare bone. Did you set down one thing you keep gnawing, even for a minute? Day four hundred forty-seven.

Do Buddhists eat meat? Ask around and you may hear three answers. Never. It depends. Whatever is offered. Each answer has its own teachers and texts behind it. The question is old. Jivaka, a physician who, tradition says, cared for a king and for the Buddha himself, once heard a rumor about the Buddha's food, and instead of repeating it, he came straight to the source to ask. Today: Jivaka and meat.
screen: `DO BUDDHISTS EAT MEAT?` → `NEVER. IT DEPENDS. WHATEVER IS OFFERED.` → `JIVAKA ASKS THE SOURCE.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-fifth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Jivaka. Jivaka says: I've heard people say that living beings are killed for the Buddha, and he knowingly eats meat prepared for him. Is that true? The Buddha says: those who say that misrepresent me. Then he gives the rule. There are three cases in which meat should not be eaten by a monk: when it's seen, heard or suspected that the animal was killed for him. In those cases, no. Otherwise, a monk who lives on alms eats what is put in his bowl, without choosing. Then he goes further. A monk who lives with loving-kindness, he says, receiving alms in a village, eats without being greedy, without being infatuated, seeing the danger in food and the escape from it. And anyone who kills a living being for the Buddha or his disciples, the Buddha says, makes much demerit: in ordering it, in the animal being dragged, in the killing, in the pain, and in offering what isn't allowable. Buddhists today live this question in different ways, and each has reasons. Theravada monks keep this three-part rule and accept what lay people offer. In Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese monasteries the custom is vegetarian, drawing on later Mahayana sutras that teach against eating meat out of compassion. In Tibetan communities practice varies, and some teachers encourage vegetarianism where it's possible. Underneath all of them sits the line Jivaka heard: no animal is to be killed for the monk. Every meal has a story behind it.
screen: `A RUMOR, AND A QUESTION` · `NOT IF SEEN, HEARD OR SUSPECTED` · `EAT WITH KINDNESS, WITHOUT GREED` · `TRADITIONS LIVE IT DIFFERENTLY` · then, large: `KNOW YOUR FOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect on today's food. Sit, and picture the last meal you ate. Follow one ingredient back: the store, the truck, the farm, the field or the animal, the hands that grew it, cut it, carried it. Don't judge. Just see how many lives touched it. Let some gratitude come, for all of it. Then think of your next meal, and ask what eating it with care might look like. The bell holds the time.
Jivaka and meat. The physician's question, and the monks' threefold rule: not if seen, heard or suspected killed for them. Today's word.
Your line: know your food. Today, at one meal, pause before the first bite and think of where it came from. Day four hundred forty-seven.

what it means: the early rule forbids meat seen, heard or suspected to be killed for the monk; later traditions went further in different ways.

448.title: Upali the householder
448.hook: a supporter of the Jain monks changes teachers; the Buddha tells him to keep feeding them
448.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Buddha's words to Upali as an example of generosity that doesn't depend on who the recipient follows; dana, giving, is practiced by lay Buddhists toward monastics and toward people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jivaka and meat, and your line, know your food. Did you pause before one bite and think of where it came from? Today, the end of a week, and a gift that keeps going. Day four hundred forty-eight.

In the town of Nalanda lives Upali, a wealthy householder and a devoted supporter of the Niganthas, the community of ascetics around the teacher Jains know as Mahavira. His house has fed their monks for years. One day a Nigantha monk comes back from talking with the Buddha, and Upali, confident, says: let me go and debate this Gotama myself. I'll drag him around like a strong man drags a ram by its fleece. His teacher agrees. Today: Upali the householder.
screen: `NALANDA. A GENEROUS HOUSEHOLDER.` → `A SUPPORTER OF THE NIGANTHAS.` → `LET ME DEBATE HIM MYSELF.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Upali. The question is: of body, speech and mind, which kind of action does the most harm? Upali's side says body. The Buddha says mind, the intention behind it all. They talk, with examples on both sides, and by the end Upali is persuaded. He asks to become the Buddha's lay follower. And here the Buddha does something surprising. He doesn't welcome him at once. He says: investigate thoroughly, Upali. It's good for a well-known man like you to think carefully first. Upali, moved, asks again. Then the Buddha says the line this story is remembered for. Your family has long been a well-spring for the Nigantha monks. You should keep giving to them when they come. Upali is struck. He'd heard that the Buddha told people to give only to him and his disciples. And here the Buddha is telling him to keep feeding the monks of the community he has just left. Upali says this makes him even more glad. This is how the Buddhist text tells the story; Jain tradition has its own texts and its own accounts of that time, and the two don't tell it the same way. But the Buddha's instruction speaks for itself. Changing your mind doesn't cancel your kindness. Old bonds of generosity are worth keeping. Look back at this week: Mara named at the door, the thicket of people, eleven doors, a hen, a bare bone, Jivaka's question. Today: a gift that keeps going.
screen: `BODY, SPEECH OR MIND: WHICH HARMS MOST?` · `INVESTIGATE THOROUGHLY FIRST` · `KEEP GIVING TO THE NIGANTHA MONKS` · `THIS WEEK: A GIFT THAT KEEPS GOING` · then, large: `KEEP GIVING TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one old kindness going. Sit, and think of a kindness you used to give that has slipped since something changed: a call to an old friend, a gift to a group you've drifted from, a neighbor you used to check on. Picture them. Notice that the change in your life didn't make them less worthy of kindness. Picture one small way to keep giving. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Upali the householder. A generous man who changed teachers, and was told by his new teacher to keep feeding the monks of his old one. Today's word.
Your line: keep giving to them. Today, keep one old kindness going, even if your life has moved on from where it started. Day four hundred forty-eight.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a generous, well-known man who has long supported another community asks to become your follower. what do you say first?
options: welcome! stop supporting them.
investigate thoroughly first.

fork.reveal: the Buddha tells Upali to investigate thoroughly. when he asks again, the Buddha accepts, and tells him to keep giving to the Nigantha monks.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana: giving, generosity. Upali's house was a well-spring of dana.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about one side winning a convert.
what it means: changing your mind doesn't cancel your kindness; the Buddha tells Upali to keep giving to his old community.

what a scholar hears: the debate turns on danda, 'rods' of body, speech and mind; the Niganthas weigh the bodily most, the Buddha the mental, which shows how central intention (cetana) is in Buddhist teaching on karma.
